hero.note: Free on macOS, Windows and Linux — a local-first mail client on the mailboxes you already own · Cloud from $9/mo, 14 days free · any IMAP mailbox, Gmail and Microsoft 365 / Exchange*. * Microsoft 365 and Exchange connect with your Microsoft sign-in on ohmail Cloud and on self-hosted servers set up for it; some organizations require an admin to approve ohmail first.

inplace.title: Your server. Your folders. Organized.
inplace.body: ohmail works on the mailboxes you already have — Metanet, Infomaniak, iCloud, Gmail, Outlook, any IMAP server. It organizes them in place: real folders on your real server, readable by any other client, forever.
inplace.compare: Where other mail apps ask you to move in with them, ohmail works where you already live.
inplace.promise: Leave anytime — your mailbox stays organized.

ai.title: AI proposes. You decide.
ai.body: Rules run first and do the bulk of the work with no AI at all — the design goal is that most of your mail is filed deterministically, by rules you can read and change. Where judgment actually helps, ohmail offers something: a door for a new sender, a draft in your voice, a nudge for a thread that went quiet. Every one of them waits for your yes, and nothing ever sends itself.
ai.status: The AI features run against a live model in production: the Screener proposes a door for a waiting sender, with a confidence and a reason, and the composer writes a first draft when you ask it for one. Both are proposals — they wait for your yes, nothing files or sends itself, and a pattern only begins running on its own once you have confirmed it often enough to graduate into a rule. The metering and spend limits that govern managed AI are in place and enforced: when the budget runs out the rules carry on, and nothing else changes.
ai.toggleBody: This is the same mail, twice. Flip the switch — nothing breaks, nothing goes missing. That is the point: ohmail is a complete mail client with the AI switched off, and a faster one with it on.
ai.captionOn: Suggestions and drafts — proposed, never performed.
ai.captionOff: Rules only. Same mail, same folders, nothing missing.
ai.rowNewOnLine: Suggested from how you handled her studio before. Press ↵ to accept.
ai.rowNewOffLine: Waiting for you — pick a door.
ai.rowReplyDraft: Ciao Giulia, perfetto — il 4 agosto va benissimo. La consegna resta all’atelier, come sempre. Grazie mille!
ai.rowReplyOnLine: Sits in the composer as a proposal. You send it, or you rewrite it, or you delete it.
ai.rowReplyOffLine: Reply — a blank composer, exactly like every other mail app.
ai.rowCodeLine: You see it in full; the code is stripped before AI reads it — in either state. Structural, not a setting.
ai.rowRuleLine: Filed by rule: list header, known newsletter. No AI in either state.
ai.pointGrad: Decide the same way three times and ohmail asks to make it a rule. You approve it once — from then on it runs deterministically, with no AI at all.
ai.pointOtp: When mail carries a verification code or login link, that code is stripped before anything reaches AI, and the mail is never forwarded and never routed automatically — structurally, with no setting to turn it off. You always see the message in full; only what a model would read is stripped.
ai.pointByoTitle: Your key, your machine — or ours
ai.pointByo: On the desktop app your mail stays on your machine, with no ohmail server in the loop — and its AI, if you want one, is your own API key or a local model, set in the app; the bill is yours. On Cloud: a monthly bag of AI credits is included, and mail keeps flowing rules-only when it runs out.

fast.title: Fast is a feature.
fast.body: Search answers as you type — typo-tolerant and scoped, over a local mirror of every mailbox — and the rest of the archive is one keystroke further, from the server. Tags instead of folder gymnastics, one tag reaching across every mailbox at once. On the desktop app your mail is already on your machine, so reading and searching work with the wifi off; in the browser that holds for the tab you have open, not for a cold start with no network.
fast.pointB: Tags, not folder trees — across every mailbox
fast.pointC: Desktop reads offline; the browser opens instantly
fast.q1Note: Typos are fine — fuzzy matching, on your own machine.
fast.q2Note: Scope it: from, tag, mailbox, before, has.
fast.q3Note: One tag, every mailbox — no folder gymnastics.

dark.title: Dark mode that includes the mail.
dark.body: Most mail arrives designed for a white screen. ohmail adapts the message itself to a dark one — same mail, same pictures, no glare — with the sender's original one click away.
dark.pointA: The whole app, light and dark — follow the system or pick one
dark.pointB: HTML mail adapted to a dark screen, not just inverted
dark.pointC: The sender's original, one click away

everyday.title: And the rest of the day.
everyday.sub: The parts you stop noticing, which is the point of them.
everyday.attachmentsBody: Open a PDF or an image inside the message. Everything else downloads, and nothing renders itself.
everyday.picturesBody: JPEGs and PNGs are compressed in your browser before they leave it, at a quality you choose — and the camera data goes with the re-encode, location included. Original sends the file as it was, and so does every other format.
everyday.trackersBody: A spy pixel is blocked by default — if you want senders to see your opens, that is a switch in Settings. One disguised as an ordinary picture loads like any picture each time the message's pictures are fetched, before it is blocked. On Cloud and on a self-hosted server, ordinary pictures load through the server's proxy, which hides your address from the sender. The desktop app and the standalone phone app fetch pictures themselves, so the sender sees that device's address.
everyday.laterBody: Send a message back to tomorrow, to next week, or to a date you pick.
everyday.unsubBody: Screen a sender out or mark them spam, and ohmail also sends the one-click unsubscribe for you — where the list offers one and the sender was confirmed by your mail provider, or by the signature the sender's own domain put on the message. On by default; a switch in Settings turns it off.
everyday.writeBody: Reply and forward with Cc and Bcc, from whichever of your mailboxes you choose.
everyday.tagsBody: One tag reaching across every mailbox. Create, rename and delete them in settings.
everyday.foldersBody: Need folders? Keep yours. Switch them on in Settings and they show in the menu, each its own list — real IMAP folders on your server, never a copy. Create, rename and delete them there too. Off until you turn it on, and not yet in the standalone desktop app.

get.title: Get ohmail.
get.sub: One product. Run it yourself for free — as a desktop app, or hosted on your own hardware — or let us run it for you. The code is public, licensed AGPL-3.0, and the hosted service is built from the same repository.
get.standaloneBody: The complete app on your machine: it connects to your own IMAP server and organizes your mailbox locally — no account, no ohmail server in the loop. macOS, Windows and Linux. Running it is already a self-hosted ohmail: the whole organizer, on hardware you own.
get.shLede: The same product on hardware you own, three ways — pick by the machine you have.
get.shServerBody: The server behind ohmail.app on a box you rent or own: prebuilt images, one compose file, no account with us — and mailboxes are unmetered.
get.shHomeBody: For an Umbrel box: the app manifest is public but still a draft — the guide separates what works today from what is still arriving.
get.shDesktopBody: One switch in Settings → Devices, and your phone opens your mail through your own computer — over Tailscale, a private tunnel between your own devices, while it is awake. On a machine that stays awake, that is your own ohmail server, around the clock.
get.wayManaged: Or we run it for you
get.managedLead: Don't want to worry about hosting?
get.managedBody: ohmail Cloud is the same product with us doing the hosting: the organizer runs on our servers and stays awake, the web app is there when you sign in, and your Android phone gets push. You pay monthly for the running, not for missing features — the options above are not demos.
get.moveTitle: Your settings live in your mailbox, and move with it.
get.moveBody: The senders you've screened, your rules, your notification choices, your away reply and your tag names are stored in the mailbox itself — versioned JSON in a bookkeeping folder of its own. Pick any option above and change your mind later: connect the same mailbox elsewhere, and ohmail finds your settings and asks before using them. Leave ohmail entirely and those decisions are still yours, in your own mailbox, in a format anything can parse.
get.moveMsgNote: The first lines of the real message, word for word — the rest is your settings, as JSON.
get.moveSpec: The format is public — read the specification

pricing.sub: Two free, complete ways to run it yourself — and under them, the same server run by us, monthly.
pricing.desktopClaim: A running desktop app is a complete, self-hosted ohmail — and can itself be the host your mobile app pairs with.
pricing.desktopStatusNote: A real mail client on macOS, Windows and Linux — the whole organizer runs on your machine, against your own IMAP server. No telemetry, no analytics. All that leaves on its own is a signed update check at launch and, where your provider does not confirm senders itself, a DNS lookup of the key a sender's domain signs its mail with.
pricing.desktopHostFeat: Serves your other devices — one switch, while it is awake
pricing.desktopCtaNote: Free — pick your platform below. Every build is the complete app.
pricing.cloudShared: The same server, run by us: your mail on the web and your phone, organized while you sleep. Push on Android, always-on processing, AI included.

pricing.selfWayServer: A box you rent or own — prebuilt images, one compose file: web app, API, organizer, Postgres
pricing.selfWayHome: A home-server box — the Umbrel package is public, still a draft
pricing.selfWayDesktop: Or no new machine at all — a running desktop app is already a self-hosted ohmail

downloads.title: Take it with you.

downloads.appleFormat: Disk image · Apple silicon and Intel

downloads.cloudLine: Prefer nothing to install? The web app is live and opens in a browser — it is part of Cloud, along with push and always-on processing.

compare.title: Your mailbox, or theirs.
compare.sub: We like the apps that rethink mail — the ones that screen senders, the ones that add AI to your inbox. They pushed the craft forward and we admire the work. What we don't like is where the organization ends up: inside someone else's app, staying behind when you go. So this table is about one axis only — whose mailbox it is.
compare.openUs: AGPL-3.0 — the apps and the server behind ohmail.app, in one public repository. Only the hosted service's billing machinery is private.
compare.openOthers: Closed source as a rule; where an app is open, the service that organizes the mail is not.
compare.addressesUs: Stays exactly where it is — ohmail connects over IMAP
compare.addressesOthers: Either your mail moves into their service, or only a provider or two qualify
compare.foldersUs: Real IMAP folders on your server, readable by any client
compare.foldersOthers: In their apps and their cloud — not on your server
compare.settingsUs: Stored in the mailbox itself, as plain JSON in an open, published format — readable anytime, by anything, and they move with the mailbox
compare.settingsOthers: Kept in their service; no export includes them
compare.leaveUs: Your mailbox stays organized, and your rules travel with it — to a server you run, to the free desktop app, or to no ohmail at all
compare.leaveOthers: An export file at best; the organization stays behind
compare.desktopUs: A real mail client with the engine inside: your mail is on your own disk, so it opens, reads and searches with no network — and the standalone install organizes your mailbox from your machine
compare.desktopOthers: A desktop window around their web app — the organizing happens in their cloud, not on your machine
compare.aiUs: Optional and gated — AI proposes, you decide; only a pattern you have confirmed often enough runs on its own
compare.aiOthers: Built into their cloud — or missing entirely
compare.note: Compared as of August 2026, from each product's own published documentation.
compare.usLine: ohmail's answer to every row is the same answer: it's your mailbox. Several of them, in fact — ohmail organizes two, five, ten IMAP mailboxes at once, drafts replies in your voice, learns your decisions into rules you can read and change, and never asks you to change your address, your provider, or your other mail apps.
compare.goodwill: These are good products made by people who care about mail. The right model is the one that fits your life, and it may not be ours — that is a fine outcome. We only insist on one thing: the choice should stay yours, and so should the mailbox.

data.title: Where your mail lives.
data.sub: Three ways to run one product. The mailbox is the master in all of them; what differs is whose machine holds the working copy.
data.desktopRuns: Your machine. No account, no ohmail server in the loop — macOS, Windows and Linux.
data.desktopCopy: On your own disk, so it reads and searches with no network. It never leaves your machine.
data.desktopAi: Optional: your own key, or a local model.
data.selfRuns: A server you run — the same open server behind ohmail.app, from one compose file.
data.selfCopy: In a database on your box, where it powers search and sync to your devices.
data.selfAi: Optional: a model you choose, hosted under your own key or one you run. Without one, everything else works.
data.cloudRuns: Our EU servers — the same server, run for you, and awake when your devices are not.
data.cloudCopy: On servers in Switzerland, encrypted at rest, up to your plan's storage; as your plan's storage fills, the bodies of your oldest messages are emptied to make room for new mail, and fetched back from your mail server when there is room again; the messages stay findable, because their headers, preview and the words search finds them by are kept. Deleted from the live database with your account.
data.cloudAi: Included in your plan and metered. When the credits run out, mail keeps flowing rules-only.
data.same: Cloud is self-hosting, done for you: the same open server, the same organizer, the same mailbox as the master. What changes is whose machine holds the copy — and that we bill for running it.
data.honest: The fine print for Cloud: it is not end-to-end encrypted. The service reads mail to file and search it, and a small number of people with production database access could technically read it. Never sold, never mined, never used for anything but serving you.
data.aiNote: AI on Cloud goes to Anthropic under commercial API terms: your mail is never used to train models, and requests are retained only briefly (currently up to 30 days); there is no zero-retention agreement yet. On every tier, a credential inside a message — a code, a login link, a reset token — is stripped before a request is built, and automatic routing skips that mail entirely. Structural, not a setting.

folders.title: This is what your IMAP looks like.
folders.sub: ohmail organizes your own mailbox by moving mail between a few plain folders — the ones you can open in any mail app, on the server you already have.
folders.inbox: Mail from people you've said yes to.
folders.junk: Your provider's own. Your spam verdicts file into it, and so do ohmail's confident spam verdicts once you let it act on confident suggestions. “Not junk” moves mail back out.
folders.sent: Your replies, left where your provider already keeps them.
folders.screener: New senders wait here until you decide where they go.
folders.reads: Newsletters and things you read when you have a minute.
folders.screened: Senders you keep — but out of the Inbox.
folders.meta: A small bookkeeping folder; some mail apps show it.
folders.note: None of this lives only inside ohmail. It is all real folders in your own account — so the day you leave, your mail is already filed where it belongs.

leave.title: Leave anytime.
leave.sub: Your mailbox is the source of truth: the folders are real IMAP folders on your server, and your rules and screened senders are one small message in it — always yours. Changing how you run ohmail is reconnecting a mailbox. Leaving is closing an app.
leave.fromCloudTerm: From Cloud to a server you run
leave.fromCloudBody: Cancel, connect the same mailbox to your own server, and ohmail finds your settings in it and asks before using them. The folders are already there.
leave.toDesktopTerm: From Cloud to the free desktop app
leave.toDesktopBody: The same reconnect, on your own machine — no export step, no transfer flow, no account to link. It works the other way round too.
leave.outBody: Your mail is already filed in folders any mail app reads. The settings message stays in your mailbox in a published format — delete it and nothing else changes.
leave.note: What travels today: screened senders, rules, notification choices, the away reply, your signature and tag names. Triage piles, Resurface timers and learned patterns stay with the install they were made on.

providers.title: If it speaks IMAP, ohmail organizes it.
providers.any: …and any IMAP mailbox, including your own server.
providers.note: Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com connect over IMAP, the way every other mailbox does. Native Exchange sync over Microsoft Graph — a different protocol, not IMAP — is on the roadmap and not shipped yet; we’ll say so here the day it is.

faq.title: Questions, answered.
faq.q1: What happens to my existing folders?
faq.a1: Nothing destructive. The folders you already have are left exactly as they are; ohmail organizes new mail into real IMAP folders on your server. Everything stays visible to any other mail client, on any device.
faq.a2: Anytime. Your mail never needs exporting — the originals live on your own server, in ordinary folders ohmail created in place, and nothing we do touches them. Be clear about what Cloud holds, though: a full copy of that mail — bodies, headers, subjects and senders — alongside your rules, tags and notes, because that is what makes search and push work. All of it is deleted from the live database with your account.
faq.a3: On Cloud: via the Claude API (Anthropic), under commercial API terms and within your plan's credits — the model runs at Anthropic, not on our servers. On the desktop app: wherever you point it — your own API key, or a local model through Ollama so nothing leaves your machine — set in the app, and off until you configure it. On a server you run: the model its operator configures — a hosted one under their own key, or one they run themselves — and without one everything else works. Either way, rules with no AI at all run first and are meant to handle most mail — and you can switch the AI off entirely without losing a single feature that files your mail.
faq.a4: The unit your plan is measured in. Actions cost what they cost us: screening a new sender or filing a message is 1 credit, a drafted reply 15. Drafting reads a whole thread and writes prose, so it costs more than sorting one message — pricing them the same would only mean charging everybody for the expensive one. When the monthly budget runs out, mail keeps flowing rules-only until the next cycle. There are no overage charges — ever.
faq.a5: Not as a matter of practice, and our admin tools do not display message content — every response the console can produce is checked by a test that writes a marker into every text column of every table and fails if any of it reaches a staff response. The database refuses them too: the console reads through a column-restricted database role that cannot select message content, and it verifies that restriction before it reads anything. The honest fine print: Cloud mail is stored unencrypted at the application level and is not end-to-end encrypted, so someone with production database access could technically read it; that access is held by very few people, and the product privacy policy will spell out who and under what conditions when it publishes. On Desktop the question doesn't arise — your mail never reaches our servers at all: the app runs as a real mail client against your own server, on macOS, Windows and Linux alike. Separately, nobody else gets to watch you read either: a spy pixel is blocked by default — loading them is a choice you would have to make in Settings — and one disguised as an ordinary picture loads like any picture each time the message's pictures are fetched, before it is blocked. On Cloud, ordinary pictures load through our own proxy, so the sender's server sees us and never your address; the desktop app and the standalone phone app fetch pictures themselves, so there the sender sees that device's address.
faq.a6: Any IMAP mailbox: your own domain at Metanet or Infomaniak, iCloud, Gmail, Outlook, a self-hosted server. If it speaks IMAP, ohmail organizes it in place. Native Exchange sync over Microsoft Graph is on the roadmap; Microsoft 365 connects over IMAP, like every other mailbox here.
faq.q7: Is there a trial for Cloud?
faq.a7: Yes — 14 days, no card. It is the whole product: rules, sync, push and the web app all run, and it comes with 500 credits so the drafts and the Screener's suggestions are yours to try. Spend those and mail keeps flowing rules-only; the monthly allowance begins when a subscription does. Desktop needs no trial at all; it is free.
faq.q8: Desktop or Cloud — what’s the real difference?
faq.a8: The same model, the same vocabulary, and deliberately not the same privacy posture — that is the honest difference. Desktop is free and fully standalone: all processing local, no account, no artificial limits. It is a real mail client on all three platforms — it connects to your own IMAP server and organizes your mailbox on your machine, and because your mail is on your own disk it is there to read with the network down. Its AI, if you want one, is your own API key or a local model through Ollama — set in the app, off until you configure it. Cloud adds the web app, push notifications, always-on processing while your computer sleeps, and AI included from $9 a month — and it holds a copy of your mail on our servers to do that. The same download does either one; which door you take is a choice inside the app. Both are open today.

siteMeta.title: ohmail — Consent-first, automated mail. and calendar.
siteMeta.description: Fully open source and self-hostable. The Screener holds first-time senders until you decide; everything you said yes to is organized in place — real folders on your real server. The desktop app is free on macOS, Windows and Linux and runs entirely on your own machine. Cloud from $9/mo adds the web app and push, with a 14-day trial and no card.
siteMeta.ogAlt: ohmail — Consent-first, automated mail. and calendar.

siteScreener.title: You decide who gets in.
siteScreener.body: The first time a stranger writes to you, they wait at the Screener — not in your inbox. One click picks the door, once, for every mail that sender ever writes: Ohbox for people, News for newsletters, Receipts for the paperwork. Or never again — which also unsubscribes you, where the list offers one click. Spam is one press too: the message moves to your mail server's own Junk folder, and that sender never asks again. Want help deciding? Switch on suggestions and ohmail proposes a door for each new sender as their mail arrives, at a price you see up front; plain newsletters and receipts it can file by itself, and a pattern you have confirmed often enough runs without asking — spam included. It deletes nothing on its own.
siteScreener.pointA: First-time senders held until you say so
siteScreener.pointB: One click picks the door — for good
siteScreener.pointC: Spam is one press — into your mail server's Junk, and the sender never asks again
siteScreener.pointD: Suggestions are optional, priced up front, and yours to accept
